original_txt: Capturing Windows 7 Credentials at Logon Using Custom Credential Provider | Tyler Wrightson's Security Blog Tyler Wrightson's Security Blog About Quotes Rand Videos Attack, Defense, Forensics, Coding\xe2\x80\xa6 Security Capturing Windows 7 Credentials at Logon Using Custom Credential\xc2 Provider January 2, 2012 \xc2\xb7 by twrightson \xc2\xb7 in backdoors, Programs \xc2\xb7 21 Comments For the Eternally Impatient The quick lowdown: I wrote a DLL capable of logging the credentials entered at logon for Windows Vista, 7 and future versions which you can download at https://github.com/tdubs/credential-provider. \xc2 The credentials are logged to a file located at c:\\cplog.txt. \xc2 Simply copy the dll to the system32 directory and run the included register.reg script to create the necessary registry settings. The Detailed Technical Information I started testing my rootkit on a windows 7 box and luckily most of it worked. \xc2 The only thing that wasn\xe2\x80\x99t working was the ability to log credentials typed in when a user first logs in to Windows. \xc2 I\xe2\x80\x99ve had a custom GINA stub dll that\xe2\x80\x99s worked great for a while that I wrote years ago, it works with Windows 2000, XP and 2003. \xc2 GINA is the Graphical Identification and Authentication component of Windows and handles the logon screen that we\xe2\x80\x99re all familiar with. \xc2 In the past you could choose to write your own GINA dll from scratch, or you could simply \xe2\x80\x98extend\xe2\x80\x99 the functionality of other GINA modules by creating a GINA stub dll. Microsoft in their infinite wisdom decided to completely change the API and move away from GINA and the GINA model. \xc2 Now to customize the logon experience you have to implement a Credential Provider, this is true for Windows Vista and newer (7 and 2008). \xc2 Microsoft claims the reasoning behind this is to make it easier for developers to meet the demands for next generation authentication technologies (like biometrics, two factor and single sign on). \xc2 Frankly in a way Credential Providers are a lot easier to work with, but in another (probably more accurate way) they\xe2\x80\x99re a huge pain in the ass to create our nefarious dll. \xc2 From what I remember creating a GINA stub dll to log Windows credentials took me probably 3 hours. \xc2 To get a credential provider to do exactly what I want took probably a good 40 hours. \xc2 At this point I should probably thank my girlfriend for putting up with my obsessive programming and constant cursing. The Credential Provider Model I won\xe2\x80\x99t go over how GINA handled the authentication process, although if i get enough requests I might detail that in another post. \xc2 Instead I\xe2\x80\x99ll focus on how the Credential Provider Model works. \xc2 Credential Providers are \xe2\x80\x98In-Process COM objects\xe2\x80\x99, aka a DLL. \xc2 Out of process COM objects would essentially be another executable that the interacting exe would interface with. \xc2 COM or Component Object Model is a pretty ethereal term, it\xe2\x80\x99s basically a binary standard and language neutral way of implementing inter process communication, among other things. \xc2 This is obviously oversimplifying it, but this isn\xe2\x80\x99t a discussion on COM. \xc2 This was my first time working with COM programming so that definitely accounts for some of the additional time. The default credential provider is the PasswordProvider that comes with Windows 7 and has a GUID of 6f45dc1e-5384-457a-bc13-2cd81b0d28ed. \xc2 GUIDs are simply unique identifiers for our COM object. \xc2 One of the most important things to understand is that Credential Providers are not responsible for actually authenticating users. \xc2 It simply gathers the necessary information, \xe2\x80\x98serializes\xe2\x80\x99 the data, and then hands off the credentials to the Local System Authority. \xc2 Serializing the data simply involves putting the username and password (and potentially other variables) in a specific format and passing them back to logonui which then hands it off to the LSA. A Tile is a new term for an important component of a Credential Provider. \xc2 Credential providers are represented by unique tiles at the logon screen, although it\xe2\x80\x99s not a one to one mapping of one tile for each Credential Provider. \xc2 For example the default password provider enumerates credentials or user accounts and creates a unique tile for each username. \xc2 The user can then click the tile for their username, type in the password and be authenticated. \xc2 Although the Credential Provider is not directly responsible for creating the graphical elements it does instruct Logonui of the fields it wishes to present to the user, this does actually make things a lot easier than programming the entire interface. In this image you\xe2\x80\x99ll see that we have two credential providers co-existing. \xc2 The default passwordprovider is on the left and our credential provider is on the right. You\xe2\x80\x99ll notice that in this scenario there\xe2\x80\x99s no way for the user to distinguish between the two credential providers. \xc2 So we need a way to \xe2\x80\x98force\xe2\x80\x99 the user into only using our credential provider. \xc2 There\xe2\x80\x99s no way to truly \xe2\x80\x98force\xe2\x80\x99 a user to use a particular credential provider when multiple credential providers are presented. \xc2 To accomplish our goal we can use the CredentialProviderFilter interface to filter out any other credential providers, more on this shortly. Winlogon.exe launches Logonui.exe which then queries the credential provider and the credential provider returns information to logonui. \xc2 The credential providers are defined in the registry and referenced by a GUID (a unique ID). \xc2 The location in the registry where credential providers are defined is: HKLM\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Authentication\\CredentialProviders. \xc2 To add a credential provider we create a new key with the GUID of the provider and copy the dll to the system32 directory. this is handled by the register.reg file included with ours. Credential Provider Wrapper We have the option of creating our own credential provider from scratch, filtering out any other provider and logging the credentials. \xc2 This isn\xe2\x80\x99t optimal for a few reasons. \xc2 Besides the fact that it\xe2\x80\x99s a considerable amount of work to create a credential provider to mimic all the existing functionality the main reason we don\xe2\x80\x99t want to do this is because we can\xe2\x80\x99t guarantee that the target system we wish to deploy our rogue credential provider on will look and feel exactly as the user expects it to. \xc2 For example if the company has deployed a new credential provider to ask the user additional questions during log in and our credential provider does not include those same questions this could set off a huge red flag for anyone using that system. Thus the best solution for us is to wrap the existing credential providers. \xc2 The new process flow with a wrapped provider looks like this figure. \xc2 Logonui will make the function calls into our custom credential provider, we can then choose to either handle processing for that function or hand it off to the wrapped credential provider. We actually have many choices on how to log the username and password using our credential provider wrapper. \xc2 The solution I chose was to manipulate the SetStringValue function. \xc2 This function is called every time a user types a key for any field in the credential provider. \xc2 Thus when a user types in a key we simply write that key to a file. \xc2 This also allows us to capture ANYTHING a user types in to a field when they logon, so our provider should grab everything for next gen or non standard credential providers. We also manipulate the\xc2 GetStringValue function which gives us the string value of fields in the credential provider. \xc2 This is handy because the default password provider does not prompt the user for their username. \xc2 Instead the user clicks a tile with their username already filled in, thus we can\xe2\x80\x99t get the username from the SetStringValue function. The implementation of my code to grab the user from the GetStringValue function demonstrates a handy feature of the way the wrapped and wrapper relationship works. \xc2 In the sample wrapper from the Windows SDK logonui calls our getstringvalue function and we simply hand the variables off directly to the wrapped credential provider. \xc2 The wrapped credential provider then performs the work of the getstringvalue function, everything works as it should, and all is good in the world. \xc2 Since the ppwsz variable we give to the wrapped credential provider is a pointer to the PWSTR variable that will contain the string of the field specified we can access this variable when the wrapped function returns. \xc2 Thus rather than implementing the getstringvalue function we simply hand off the variables as usual and print out the string from the pointer after the real function does all the work and returns. The function for handing off the work for the GetStringValue function to our wrapped provider looks like this; hr = _pWrappedCredential->GetStringValue(dwFieldID, ppwsz); CredentialProviderFilter As part of the custom credential provider I implemented the credential provider filter. \xc2 This might be one of the most helpful parts of this project/post for other developers. \xc2 Microsoft has an FAQ included with their SDK samples for Credential Providers that states they will NOT release a sample credential provider filter\xe2\x80\xa6 Thanks Microsoft for releasing a complex API and offering ZERO help, terrific. Luckily I was able to find a broken example online, fix it, fill in some gaps and now it\xe2\x80\x99s fully functional. \xc2 Thank you to the anonymous person who started the effort. \xc2 Credential Providers are defined in the registry as well at\xc2 HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Authentication\\Credential Provider Filters\\. \xc2 Again all you have to do is create a key with the GUID of the filter. \xc2 This is included in the register.reg file included with my credential provider. Logonui will call the Filter function for any configured credential provider filters. \xc2 It will pass a BOOL variable for every credential provider configured, at which point the Filter can choose to allow or deny the specified credential provider by setting the BOOL variable to true or false. Currently my filter only filters out the password provider, but it\xe2\x80\x99s incredibly easy to change it to filter out all other providers. \xc2 The following evaluation checks to see if the credential provider GUID matches that of the default password provider, if so it filters it out by setting the rgbAllow BOOL to FALSE. \xc2 You could change this evaluation to always be true and filter out all providers. if (IsEqualGUID(rgclsidProviders[i], CLSID_PasswordCredentialProvider)) rgbAllow[i] = FALSE; Special Notes about The Credential Provider Wrapper I originally had some issues when trying to compile on Visual Studio 2010 Express so I used Visual Studio 2008 Express and everything was fine. \xc2 I have no doubt you could get this to compile with 2010, I just didn\xe2\x80\x99t feel like wasting time on it. \xc2 In addition I had to use the _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS\xc2 preprocessor settings which are defined under the properties for the project in Visual Studio, under C/C++ -> Preprocessor Definitions. \xc2 This allows us to use the fopen function rather than fopen_s, again, just laziness on my side. \xc2 If Microsoft wants to force me to use a specific function it makes me want to do it less, just\xc2 stubbornness from my childhood that\xe2\x80\x99s stuck. I also had to use the following two defines to suppress the error 4995. #define DEPRECATE_SUPPORTED #pragma warning(disable:4995) The GUID can be changed to whatever you want, just manipulate the define in the guid.h file. \xc2 One of the best resources I found for helping to understand development of a credential provider was the \xe2\x80\x98Credential Provider Technical Doc.doc\xe2\x80\x99, I\xe2\x80\x99ve included a copy of this doc in my full archive for the credential provider in case the link is ever broken on the interwebs. \xc2 You can download the source and dll at\xc2 https://github.com/tdubs/credential-provider\xc2 https://github.com/tdubs/credential-provider/blob/master/cp-devel.zip Share this: Twitter Facebook Like this: Like Loading... We actually have many choices on how to log the username and password using our credential provider wrapper. \xc2 The solution I chose was to manipulate the SetStringValue function. \xc2 This function is called every time a user types a key for any field in the credential provider. \xc2 Thus when a user types in a key we simply write that key to a file. \xc2 This also allows us to capture ANYTHING a user types in to a field when they logon, so our provider should grab everything for next gen or non standard credential providers. We also manipulate the\xc2 GetStringValue function which gives us the string value of fields in the credential provider. \xc2 This is handy because the default password provider does not prompt the user for their username. \xc2 Instead the user clicks a tile with their username already filled in, thus we can\xe2\x80\x99t get the username from the SetStringValue function. The implementation of my code to grab the user from the GetStringValue function demonstrates a handy feature of the way the wrapped and wrapper relationship works. \xc2 In the sample wrapper from the Windows SDK logonui calls our getstringvalue function and we simply hand the variables off directly to the wrapped credential provider. \xc2 The wrapped credential provider then performs the work of the getstringvalue function, everything works as it should, and all is good in the world. \xc2 Since the ppwsz variable we give to the wrapped credential provider is a pointer to the PWSTR variable that will contain the string of the field specified we can access this variable when the wrapped function returns. \xc2 Thus rather than implementing the getstringvalue function we simply hand off the variables as usual and print out the string from the pointer after the real function does all the work and returns. The function for handing off the work for the GetStringValue function to our wrapped provider looks like this; hr = _pWrappedCredential->GetStringValue(dwFieldID, ppwsz); CredentialProviderFilter As part of the custom credential provider I implemented the credential provider filter. \xc2 This might be one of the most helpful parts of this project/post for other developers. \xc2 Microsoft has an FAQ included with their SDK samples for Credential Providers that states they will NOT release a sample credential provider filter\xe2\x80\xa6 Thanks Microsoft for releasing a complex API and offering ZERO help, terrific. Luckily I was able to find a broken example online, fix it, fill in some gaps and now it\xe2\x80\x99s fully functional. \xc2 Thank you to the anonymous person who started the effort. \xc2 Credential Providers are defined in the registry as well at\xc2 HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Authentication\\Credential Provider Filters\\. \xc2 Again all you have to do is create a key with the GUID of the filter. \xc2 This is included in the register.reg file included with my credential provider. Logonui will call the Filter function for any configured credential provider filters. \xc2 It will pass a BOOL variable for every credential provider configured, at which point the Filter can choose to allow or deny the specified credential provider by setting the BOOL variable to true or false. Currently my filter only filters out the password provider, but it\xe2\x80\x99s incredibly easy to change it to filter out all other providers. \xc2 The following evaluation checks to see if the credential provider GUID matches that of the default password provider, if so it filters it out by setting the rgbAllow BOOL to FALSE. \xc2 You could change this evaluation to always be true and filter out all providers. if (IsEqualGUID(rgclsidProviders[i], CLSID_PasswordCredentialProvider)) rgbAllow[i] = FALSE; Special Notes about The Credential Provider Wrapper I originally had some issues when trying to compile on Visual Studio 2010 Express so I used Visual Studio 2008 Express and everything was fine. \xc2 I have no doubt you could get this to compile with 2010, I just didn\xe2\x80\x99t feel like wasting time on it. \xc2 In addition I had to use the _CRT_SECURE_NO_WARNINGS\xc2 preprocessor settings which are defined under the properties for the project in Visual Studio, under C/C++ -> Preprocessor Definitions. \xc2 This allows us to use the fopen function rather than fopen_s, again, just laziness on my side. \xc2 If Microsoft wants to force me to use a specific function it makes me want to do it less, just\xc2 stubbornness from my childhood that\xe2\x80\x99s stuck. I also had to use the following two defines to suppress the error 4995. #define DEPRECATE_SUPPORTED #pragma warning(disable:4995) The GUID can be changed to whatever you want, just manipulate the define in the guid.h file. \xc2 One of the best resources I found for helping to understand development of a credential provider was the \xe2\x80\x98Credential Provider Technical Doc.doc\xe2\x80\x99, I\xe2\x80\x99ve included a copy of this doc in my full archive for the credential provider in case the link is ever broken on the interwebs. \xc2 You can download the source and dll at\xc2 https://github.com/tdubs/credential-provider\xc2 https://github.com/tdubs/credential-provider/blob/master/cp-devel.zip Share this: Twitter Facebook Like this: Like Loading...
